notes.title: 1.1 Definitions and Scope of Economics
notes.content:
• The word economics comes from the Greek words oikos (household) and nomos (management/rules) — literally "household management".
• Economics is the social science that studies how individuals, firms, governments and societies use limited (scarce) resources to satisfy unlimited human wants.
• Four main schools of definition:
• 1. Wealth Definition — Adam Smith (1776), "An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations"
– Economics is the science of wealth; it studies how a nation becomes rich.
– Focus: production, accumulation and distribution of wealth. Smith is called the Father of Economics.
– Other supporters: J.B. Say, J.S. Mill, Walker.
– Criticism: treats wealth as the end rather than a means; ignores human welfare; Carlyle called economics the "dismal science" because of its stress on wealth.
• 2. Welfare Definition — Alfred Marshall (1890), "Principles of Economics"
– "Economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life; it examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and with the use of the material requisites of well-being."
– Wealth is only a means to human welfare. Focus on material welfare of ordinary people. Supporters: Pigou, Cannan, Beveridge.
– Features: studies ordinary people; studies material welfare only; economics is a social science; wealth is a means, not an end.
– Criticism: distinction between material and non-material welfare is artificial; welfare cannot be measured exactly; ignores services of teachers, doctors, singers (non-material); does not explain scarcity.
• 3. Scarcity Definition — Lionel Robbins (1932), "An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science"
– "Economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses."
– Four key elements: (i) unlimited wants/ends; (ii) scarce means (limited resources); (iii) alternative uses of resources; (iv) choice — because of scarcity, one must choose.
– Economics is neutral between ends — it does not judge whether a want is good or bad.
– Criticism: too narrow, ignores welfare; ignores problems of growth and unemployment; makes economics purely a positive science; ignores normative aspects; scarcity is not the only cause of economic problems.
• 4. Growth (Dynamic) Definition — Paul A. Samuelson
– "Economics is the study of how men and society choose, with or without the use of money, to employ scarce productive resources which could have alternative uses, to produce various commodities over time and distribute them for consumption, now or in the future, among various people and groups of society."
– Adds the time dimension (growth, development) and covers barter economies too. Considered the most complete modern definition.
• Scope of economics (what it covers):
– Subject matter: consumption, production, exchange (trade), distribution (rent, wages, interest, profit) and public finance.
– Micro and macro divisions: study of individual units vs the whole economy.
– Positive and normative: what is vs what ought to be.
– Is economics a science or an art? Science — systematic body of knowledge, cause-effect relations (though it is a social, not exact, science). Art — gives practical guidance for solving problems (e.g. policy making). Today it is regarded as both.
– Relationship with other subjects: political science (public policy), sociology (social behaviour), history (past data), mathematics and statistics (econometrics), psychology (consumer behaviour), ethics (welfare), law (property rights).
– Limitations of scope: human behaviour is unpredictable; controlled experiments are difficult; "ceteris paribus" (other things being equal) is an assumption that rarely holds exactly.

notes.title: 1.2 Importance of Studying Economics
notes.content:
• Helps understand how scarce resources are best allocated — key to solving the basic economic problem.
• Helps consumers make rational choices about spending and saving to maximise satisfaction.
• Helps producers decide what, how much and how to produce at least cost and maximum profit.
• Helps workers/trade unions understand wages, productivity and employment.
• Helps government frame policies — fiscal policy (taxes, spending), monetary policy (money supply, interest rates), trade policy, planning.
• Helps understand national problems: poverty, unemployment, inflation, inequality, regional imbalance, population growth.
• Helps understand international issues: exchange rates, balance of payments, WTO, globalisation.
• Develops analytical and logical thinking; useful in business, banking, civil services, journalism, law, research.
• Helps in economic planning and forecasting; guides in understanding economic growth versus economic development.
• Promotes social welfare by showing how income and wealth can be distributed more equitably.

notes.title: 1.3 Nature of Economics: Positive vs Normative Science
notes.content:
• Positive economics: deals with "what is", "what was", "what will be". Based on facts, can be tested and verified with data. Free from value judgements.
– Examples: "India's GDP grew by 7% last year"; "If the price of petrol rises, demand will fall"; "Unemployment rate is 8%".
• Normative economics: deals with "what ought to be". Based on opinions, ethics and value judgements. Cannot be proved true or false by data alone.
– Examples: "The government should reduce income inequality"; "Minimum wage should be raised"; "Rich people should be taxed more".
[TABLE]
Basis | Positive Economics | Normative Economics
Concerns | What is / what will be | What ought to be
Nature | Factual, objective | Judgemental, subjective
Testing | Can be verified by facts | Cannot be verified purely by facts
Keywords | Is, will, would | Should, ought, must
Role | Explains cause and effect | Prescribes policy and goals
Linked with | Robbins' view of economics | Marshall/Pigou welfare view
[/TABLE]
• Both are interdependent: policy (normative) needs analysis of facts (positive).
• Economics as a science: has laws (law of demand, law of diminishing returns), uses scientific method (observation, hypothesis, testing, conclusion), but laws are tendencies, not exact like physical sciences, because human behaviour varies.
• Economic laws are hypothetical (based on "if... then") and are statements of tendencies.
• Methods of economic analysis: deductive (general to particular — logic, assumptions), inductive (particular to general — data, observation).
• Ceteris paribus = "other things remaining constant" — basic assumption used to isolate effect of one variable.

notes.title: 1.4 Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics
notes.content:
• Terms coined by Ragnar Frisch (1933): micro = small, macro = large.
• Microeconomics: study of individual economic units — a consumer, household, firm, industry, a single market.
– Topics: demand and supply, price determination, consumer behaviour, production, cost, market structures, factor pricing (wages, rent, interest, profit), welfare economics.
– Also called price theory. Main tool: marginal analysis. Method: partial equilibrium analysis (one market at a time).
– Central problem: price determination and allocation of resources.
• Macroeconomics: study of the economy as a whole — aggregates like national income, total employment, general price level, money supply, savings, investment, balance of payments.
– Also called income and employment theory. Associated with J.M. Keynes ("General Theory", 1936).
– Central problem: determination of national income and employment, inflation, growth.
– Method: aggregative analysis (the economy is studied through totals and averages such as total output and the general price level).
[TABLE]
Basis | Microeconomics | Macroeconomics
Meaning | Study of individual units | Study of whole economy
Subject matter | Price, demand, supply, cost | National income, employment, inflation, growth
Also called | Price theory | Income and employment theory
Approach | Partial equilibrium (one market at a time) | Aggregative (whole-economy) analysis
Policy | Price/allocation policy | Fiscal and monetary policy
Example | Demand for cars | Overall unemployment
[/TABLE]
• Paradox of thrift and fallacy of composition show the two are linked: what is true for the individual need not be true for the whole.
• Limitations of micro: ignores whole-economy interlinkages; limitations of macro: ignores individual differences and structure.

notes.title: 1.5 Fundamental Problems of an Economy — Optimum Allocation of Resources
notes.content:
• Root cause: scarcity of resources + unlimited wants + alternative uses of resources = problem of choice.
• Features of wants: unlimited; recurring; vary in intensity; satisfiable individually (a single want can be satisfied); competitive and complementary; become habits.
• Types of resources (factors of production): land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship.
• The Central (Basic) Problems:
– 1. What to produce and in what quantity? — consumer goods vs capital goods; necessities vs luxuries; civil vs military goods; present vs future consumption.
– 2. How to produce? — choice of technique: labour-intensive vs capital-intensive; large scale vs small scale. Decided by relative factor prices and efficiency (least-cost combination).
– 3. For whom to produce? — distribution of national product among people; depends on income distribution (wages, rent, interest, profit); issue of equity.
– 4. Are resources being fully and efficiently utilised? — problem of unemployment/idle resources and efficiency.
– 5. Is the economy growing? — problem of economic growth and development; savings and investment for the future.
• The first three are the basic allocation problems; the last two are problems of employment/efficiency and growth.
• How different economic systems solve them:
– Capitalist (market) economy: solved by price mechanism; private ownership; profit motive; consumer sovereignty (e.g. USA).
– Socialist (command) economy: solved by central planning authority; state ownership (e.g. erstwhile USSR, China earlier).
– Mixed economy: both private and public sectors co-exist; market plus government regulation (e.g. India, UK, France).
• Optimum (efficient) allocation of resources: using resources so that no reallocation can make someone better off without making someone worse off (Pareto efficiency). Requires productive efficiency (production at lowest cost — on the PPC) and allocative efficiency (producing what society wants — where price = marginal cost).

notes.title: 1.6 Opportunity Cost and Production Possibility Curve (PPC)
notes.content:
• Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It is the real cost of any decision. Also called alternative cost or economic cost.
– Examples: using a plot for a school means giving up its use as a park; a student spending 3 hours studying gives up 3 hours of wages.
– Opportunity cost is not always money; it is the benefit lost.
– Arises because of scarcity and choice. Zero for free goods (air).
• Production Possibility Curve (PPC) / Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) / Transformation Curve: shows the different maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources and technology, assuming full employment and efficient use.
• Assumptions: only two goods; resources fixed in supply; technology constant; resources are fully and efficiently employed; resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods.
• Illustration (schedule):
[TABLE]
Combination | Wheat (million tonnes) | Cloth (million metres) | MOC of 1 tonne wheat
A | 0 | 15 | —
B | 1 | 14 | 1 metre cloth
C | 2 | 12 | 2 metres cloth
D | 3 | 9 | 3 metres cloth
E | 4 | 5 | 4 metres cloth
F | 5 | 0 | 5 metres cloth
[/TABLE]
• Shape: concave to the origin (bowed outward) because of the increasing marginal opportunity cost — as more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be shifted, so more of the other good must be given up per extra unit.
• Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT) = slope of PPC = units of Y sacrificed per extra unit of X = ΔY/ΔX.
• Points on the PPC: efficient, full employment of resources. Inside the PPC: unemployment/inefficient use of resources — attainable but not efficient. Outside the PPC: unattainable with present resources and technology.
• Shifts of PPC:
– Outward (rightward) shift: economic growth — more resources, better technology, education, capital accumulation.
– Inward shift: loss of resources — war, natural disasters, population decline.
– Pivotal shift (rotation): technology improves in only one good — only that axis intercept changes.
• Straight-line PPC: constant opportunity cost (resources perfectly substitutable). Convex PPC: decreasing opportunity cost (rare).
• Uses of PPC: illustrates scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, unemployment, growth, and the central problems of what to produce.
• Distinction: movement along the PPC = reallocating resources between goods; shift of PPC = change in productive capacity.

notes.title: 2.1 Definition of Utility and Marginal Utility; Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
notes.content:
• Utility: the want-satisfying power of a commodity; the satisfaction a consumer derives from consuming a good or service.
• Features of utility: subjective (varies person to person); relative (varies with time, place and person); not the same as usefulness; not the same as pleasure; has no moral meaning (cigarettes have utility for a smoker); can be measured in utils (cardinal approach).
• Forms of utility (Prof. Marshall): form utility, place utility, time utility, service utility, possession utility.
• Two approaches to measuring utility:
– Cardinal approach (Marshall): utility can be measured in numbers called utils. Basis of marginal utility analysis.
– Ordinal approach (Hicks and Allen): utility cannot be measured but can be ranked (first, second, third preference). Basis of indifference curve analysis.
• Total Utility (TU): the sum of utilities obtained from consuming all units of a commodity. TU = ΣMU.
• Marginal Utility (MU): the addition to total utility from consuming one more unit. MU = ΔTU/ΔQ, or MUn = TUn − TUn−1.
• Average Utility (AU) = TU/Q.
• Relationship between TU and MU:
– When MU is positive and falling, TU rises at a diminishing rate.
– When MU = 0, TU is at its maximum (point of satiety).
– When MU is negative, TU falls (disutility).
• Illustration:
[TABLE]
Units of bread | TU (utils) | MU (utils)
1 | 30 | 30
2 | 50 | 20
3 | 62 | 12
4 | 68 | 6
5 | 68 | 0
6 | 62 | −6
[/TABLE]
• Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility (Gossen's First Law): as a consumer consumes more units of a commodity, the marginal utility from each additional unit goes on diminishing, other things remaining constant. (Stated by H.H. Gossen; developed by Marshall.)
• Assumptions: utility is measurable in cardinal numbers; consumption is continuous (no gap in time); units are identical (homogeneous) and of standard size; tastes, habits and income remain unchanged; MU of money is constant; consumer is rational; no change in prices of related goods.
• Explanation: the first unit satisfies the most urgent want; later units satisfy less intense wants.
• Exceptions/limitations: hobbies and collection (stamps, coins); drunkards and misers (money, liquor); reading of a language or music (more practice may raise utility); display of rare art; very small units (a drop of water); love and affection.
• Importance: basis of the law of demand; explains downward-sloping demand curve; explains diamond–water paradox (water has high total utility but low marginal utility due to abundance; diamonds the opposite); basis of progressive taxation (MU of money falls as income rises); basis of consumer surplus; explains why price falls as supply increases.
• Law of Equi-Marginal Utility (Gossen's Second Law): a rational consumer allocates income among goods so that the MU per rupee spent is equal across goods: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = … = MUm (marginal utility of money).
– Assumptions: same as DMU, plus limited income, and utility of goods is independent.
– If MUx/Px > MUy/Py, buy more X and less Y until equal.
– Applications: consumption, production (factor allocation), public finance, saving vs spending.
• Consumer surplus (Marshall): difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what he actually pays. CS = total utility − (price × quantity). Arises from diminishing MU. Concept limitations: utility not measurable; MU of money not constant; ignores substitutes; no surplus for necessities of life in a strict sense (diamond–water).

notes.title: 2.2 Indifference Curve and Budget Constraint
notes.content:
• Indifference curve (IC): a curve showing all combinations of two goods that give the consumer equal satisfaction; the consumer is indifferent among them. Introduced by Edgeworth, developed by Hicks and Allen (1934); earlier by Pareto.
• Indifference schedule example:
[TABLE]
Combination | Apples | Oranges
A | 1 | 12
B | 2 | 8
C | 3 | 5
D | 4 | 3
E | 5 | 2
[/TABLE]
• Indifference map: a set of indifference curves; higher IC = higher satisfaction.
• Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRSxy): the rate at which a consumer is willing to give up units of Y for one more unit of X, keeping total satisfaction constant. MRS = −ΔY/ΔX = MUx/MUy. Diminishing MRS is why IC is convex to the origin.
• Properties of IC:
– 1. Slopes downward from left to right (more of one good means less of the other).
– 2. Convex to the origin (diminishing MRS).
– 3. Two ICs never intersect (it would violate transitivity and consistency).
– 4. Higher IC represents higher satisfaction (more of at least one good).
– 5. ICs do not touch the axes (consumer consumes both goods).
– 6. ICs need not be parallel.
• Assumptions of IC analysis: rationality; ordinal utility; non-satiation (more is better); diminishing MRS; transitivity/consistency of preferences; given tastes and income.
• Special shapes: perfect substitutes — straight line, negative slope, constant MRS (e.g. two brands of identical pens). Perfect complements — L-shaped (e.g. left and right shoes). Neutral good/bad — vertical/horizontal or upward-sloping lines.
• Budget constraint / budget line (price line): shows all combinations of two goods a consumer can buy with a given income and given prices. Equation: M = Px·X + Py·Y.
– Intercepts: X-axis = M/Px; Y-axis = M/Py. Slope = −Px/Py (price ratio).
– Example: income Rs. 100, Px = Rs. 10, Py = Rs. 20 — maximum X = 10, maximum Y = 5.
– Points on the line: affordable and exhaust income; inside: affordable but income left; outside: unaffordable.
• Shifts of the budget line: increase in income — parallel outward shift; decrease in income — parallel inward shift; fall in Px — pivots outward on the X-axis (flatter); rise in Px — pivots inward; same for Py on Y-axis; equal proportional change in both prices — parallel shift.
• Differences — cardinal vs ordinal approach: cardinal assumes measurable utility, constant MU of money, uses MU curves; ordinal needs only ranking, no constant MU of money, uses IC and budget lines; ordinal is considered more realistic.

notes.title: 2.3 Consumer Equilibrium
notes.content:
• Consumer equilibrium: the situation in which a consumer maximises satisfaction from given income and prices and has no tendency to change his consumption pattern.
• Cardinal (Marginal Utility) approach:
– Single commodity: consumer is in equilibrium where MU of the commodity = Price (in terms of MU of money): MUx = Px. If MU > P buy more; if MU < P buy less.
– Two or more commodities: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MUm. Illustration with table: equilibrium reached when marginal utility per rupee is equal for both goods and the whole income is spent.
• Ordinal (Indifference curve) approach: the consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve.
– First-order (necessary) condition: slope of IC = slope of budget line, i.e. MRSxy = Px/Py (equivalent to MUx/MUy = Px/Py, giving MUx/Px = MUy/Py).
– Second-order (sufficient) condition: IC must be convex to the origin at the point of tangency (MRS is diminishing).
– Why not other points? On a lower IC the consumer can still reach higher satisfaction; a higher IC is out of reach; at intersection points of IC and budget line, moving along the budget line reaches a higher IC.
• Corner solution: consumer spends all income on only one good (budget line touches IC at an axis). Happens when MRS never equals the price ratio (e.g. perfect substitutes with unequal price ratio).
• Effects of changes:
– Income-consumption curve (ICC): locus of equilibrium points as income changes, prices constant. Positive slope for normal goods; backward-bending for inferior goods. Engel curve relates income to quantity demanded.
– Price-consumption curve (PCC): locus of equilibrium points as the price of one good changes. Used to derive the demand curve.
• Derivation of demand curve using IC: each price of X gives a different budget line and a different equilibrium on the PCC; plotting price against quantity bought gives the downward-sloping demand curve.
• Price effect = Substitution effect + Income effect.
– Substitution effect: change in consumption because of change in relative price, keeping real income constant — always negative.
– Income effect: change in consumption due to change in real income — positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods.
– Giffen goods: inferior goods with negative income effect strong enough to outweigh substitution effect — demand curve slopes upward.

notes.title: 3.1 Demand: Meaning, Determinants, Deriving Demand Curve — Individual vs Market
notes.content:
• Demand = the quantity of a commodity a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price during a given period of time. Demand requires: (i) desire, (ii) ability to pay (purchasing power), (iii) willingness to spend, (iv) price, (v) time period.
• Demand is not the same as desire or need — desire without purchasing power is not demand.
• Demand function: Qd = f(Px, Pr, Y, T, E, N, …) — i.e. demand depends on own price, price of related goods, income, tastes, expectations, population.
• Determinants of demand:
– 1. Price of the commodity: inverse relation (law of demand).
– 2. Price of related goods: substitutes (tea–coffee): price of one rises, demand for the other rises. Complements (car–petrol): price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
– 3. Income of the consumer: normal goods — demand rises with income; inferior goods — demand falls with income (coarse grain); necessities — demand rises slowly; luxuries — demand rises faster.
– 4. Tastes, fashion and habits.
– 5. Expectations of future price and income.
– 6. Population size and composition (age, sex, urban/rural).
– 7. Distribution of income — more equal distribution increases demand for necessities.
– 8. Government policy — taxes, subsidies, rationing.
– 9. Climate/season, advertising, credit facilities, availability of substitutes, business conditions.
• Types of demand: Individual demand (one consumer); Market demand (sum of all individual demands); Direct vs derived demand (demand for food vs demand for steel to make cars); Joint (complementary) demand; Composite demand (a good with multiple uses — steel); Competitive demand (substitutes); Autonomous vs induced demand; Price, income and cross demand.
• Demand schedule: a table showing quantity demanded at different prices. Individual demand schedule for one consumer; market demand schedule is a horizontal sum.
[TABLE]
Price (Rs.) | Consumer A | Consumer B | Consumer C | Market demand
10 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 3
8 | 2 | 1 | 3 | 6
6 | 3 | 2 | 4 | 9
4 | 4 | 3 | 5 | 12
[/TABLE]
• Demand curve: graphical representation of the demand schedule — price on Y axis, quantity on X axis; slopes downward from left to right.
• Deriving the individual demand curve: from the demand schedule (plot points and join) or from consumer equilibrium: using the marginal utility approach (MU = P — the MU curve is the demand curve, because the consumer buys until MU = price) or the IC approach (price-consumption curve).
• Deriving the market demand curve: horizontal summation of all individual demand curves at each price.
• Differences: the individual curve is usually steeper; the market curve is flatter and smoother as more consumers join at lower prices; the market curve is also affected by population, income distribution and number of consumers.

notes.title: 3.2 Law of Demand and Exceptions
notes.content:
• Law of Demand: other things remaining the same (ceteris paribus), when the price of a commodity falls, its quantity demanded rises, and when price rises, quantity demanded falls — an inverse relationship between price and quantity. (Marshall.)
• Assumptions: no change in consumer's income; no change in tastes and fashion; no change in prices of related goods; no expectation of future price change; no change in population; no change in government policy; normal commodity.
• Reasons for the downward slope:
– Law of diminishing marginal utility — consumer buys more only at a lower price.
– Income effect — fall in price raises real income, so more is bought.
– Substitution effect — cheaper good replaces costlier substitutes.
– New consumers — lower price attracts new buyers.
– Multiple uses of a commodity (milk, electricity).
• Exceptions to the law of demand:
– Giffen goods (Sir Robert Giffen) — inferior goods taking a large part of income (coarse bread/cereals): price falls, demand falls.
– Veblen goods / conspicuous consumption (Thorstein Veblen) — diamonds, luxury cars, designer goods bought for prestige; higher price increases demand.
– Expectation of price changes — if prices are expected to rise further, people buy more now.
– Necessities of life — demand does not change much.
– Speculative markets — shares, gold, real estate: rising prices attract more buyers.
– Ignorance — consumers judge quality by price.
– Fashions, emergencies (war, famine), habitual goods (addictions).
• Demand curve shape: normally downward sloping (negative slope); upward sloping for exceptions.

notes.title: 3.3 Change in Quantity Demanded (Movement along DC) vs Change in Demand (Shift in DC)
notes.content:
• Change in quantity demanded — caused only by change in the price of the commodity, all other factors constant. Shown by movement along the same demand curve.
– Extension of demand: price falls, quantity demanded rises — downward movement.
– Contraction of demand: price rises, quantity demanded falls — upward movement.
• Change in demand — caused by change in any factor other than price (income, tastes, price of related goods, expectations, population). Shown by a shift of the entire demand curve.
– Increase in demand: rightward shift — more is demanded at each price.
– Decrease in demand: leftward shift — less is demanded at each price.
[TABLE]
Basis | Change in Quantity Demanded | Change in Demand
Cause | Change in own price only | Change in other determinants
Shown by | Movement along same curve | Shift of the curve
Terms | Extension / Contraction | Increase / Decrease
Price role | Price is the cause | Price is constant
[/TABLE]
• Causes of an increase in demand: rise in income (normal goods); rise in price of substitutes; fall in price of complements; favourable change in taste; expectation of price rise; growth in population; advertising.
• Causes of decrease in demand: opposite of the above.

notes.title: 3.4 Elasticity of Demand and its Applications
notes.content:
• Elasticity of demand: the degree of responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in one of its determinants. Concept introduced by Alfred Marshall.
• Types: (1) Price elasticity (Ed); (2) Income elasticity (Ey); (3) Cross elasticity (Ec); (4) Advertising/promotional elasticity.
• Price elasticity of demand (Ed): percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price.
– Ed = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P) = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) — usually ignoring the negative sign (absolute value).
• Degrees (types) of price elasticity:
[TABLE]
Type | Value | Description | Curve | Example
Perfectly elastic | Ed = ∞ | Infinite response to a tiny price change | Horizontal | Perfect competition firm
Perfectly inelastic | Ed = 0 | Quantity unchanged when price changes | Vertical | Life-saving drugs
Unitary elastic | Ed = 1 | % change Q = % change P | Rectangular hyperbola | —
Relatively elastic | Ed > 1 | Q changes proportionately more | Flat | Luxuries
Relatively inelastic | Ed < 1 | Q changes proportionately less | Steep | Necessities (salt)
[/TABLE]
• Methods of measuring price elasticity:
– 1. Percentage (proportionate) method: Ed = % change in Q ÷ % change in P.
– 2. Total outlay (expenditure) method (Marshall): if price falls and total expenditure rises, Ed > 1; if it stays the same, Ed = 1; if it falls, Ed < 1. (Opposite for a price rise.)
– 3. Point (geometric) method: Ed = lower segment ÷ upper segment of the demand curve at that point (for a straight-line curve). At the midpoint Ed = 1; above the midpoint Ed > 1; below Ed < 1; at the Y intercept Ed = ∞; at X intercept Ed = 0.
– 4. Arc method: used when the change is large — Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × [(P1+P2)/(Q1+Q2)] (mid-point formula).
• Numerical examples:
– Price falls from Rs. 10 to Rs. 8 and quantity rises from 100 to 120: %ΔQ = 20%, %ΔP = −20%, so Ed = 1 (unitary).
– Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 25; demand falls from 80 to 60: %ΔQ = 25%, %ΔP = 25%, Ed = 1.
– Price falls from Rs. 5 to Rs. 4; quantity rises from 50 to 80: %ΔQ = 60%, %ΔP = 20%, Ed = 3 (elastic).
• Factors affecting price elasticity: nature of the good (necessity, comfort, luxury); availability of substitutes (more substitutes means more elastic); proportion of income spent (small proportion — inelastic); time period (long run — more elastic); habits; number of uses; level of price (very high or very low prices — inelastic); postponement possibility; income level of consumers; joint demand.
• Income elasticity (Ey) = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔY. Positive for normal goods (>1 luxuries, <1 necessities); negative for inferior goods; zero for neutral goods.
• Cross elasticity (Ec) = %ΔQx ÷ %ΔPy. Positive for substitutes; negative for complements; zero for unrelated goods.
• Relationship between Ed, total revenue and marginal revenue: MR = P(1 − 1/Ed). When Ed > 1, MR > 0 and a price cut raises TR. When Ed = 1, MR = 0 and TR is at its maximum. When Ed < 1, MR < 0 and a price cut lowers TR.
• Importance and applications:
– Producers — pricing decisions (lower price for elastic goods, higher for inelastic goods), price discrimination.
– Government — tax policy (tax goods with inelastic demand: petrol, tobacco, liquor for revenue); subsidies; minimum support prices.
– Monopolist — a profit-maximising monopolist never operates on the inelastic part of demand (MR would be negative); international trade — terms of trade; exchange rates — devaluation succeeds if demand for exports is elastic (Marshall–Lerner condition: sum of elasticities > 1); factor pricing — wages in inelastic demand for labour; trade unions; tax incidence — burden falls more on the side with inelastic demand; paradox of poverty — a bumper crop may reduce farmers' income since demand for food is inelastic.

notes.title: 4.1 Supply: Meaning and Determinants
notes.content:
• Supply: the quantity of a commodity that a producer/seller is willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a given period of time.
• Supply is different from stock (total quantity available) — supply is the part of stock actually offered for sale at a price.
• Supply function: Qs = f(P, C, T, Pr, G, N, E …) — own price, cost of production/input prices, technology, prices of related goods, government policy (taxes, subsidies), number of sellers, expectations, natural conditions.
• Determinants of supply:
– 1. Price of the commodity: direct relation — higher price, higher supply.
– 2. Cost of production / prices of factor inputs: higher costs reduce supply (supply curve shifts left).
– 3. State of technology: improved technology lowers cost and increases supply.
– 4. Prices of related goods: if the price of a substitute-in-production (e.g. wheat vs. barley for farmers) rises, supply of the other falls.
– 5. Government policy: taxes reduce supply; subsidies increase supply.
– 6. Number of firms in the industry: more firms mean more market supply.
– 7. Expectations about future prices: expecting higher prices tomorrow, sellers hold back supply today.
– 8. Natural factors: weather, rainfall, disasters (especially in agriculture).
– 9. Goals of the firm: profit maximisation vs sales maximisation.
– 10. Transport and communication facilities, infrastructure, trade policy.
• Supply schedule: table of price and quantity supplied. Individual supply (one firm); market supply (sum of all firms' supplies).
[TABLE]
Price (Rs.) | Firm A | Firm B | Firm C | Market supply
10 | 10 | 5 | 10 | 25
8 | 8 | 4 | 8 | 20
6 | 6 | 3 | 5 | 14
4 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 6
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 4.2 Law of Supply and Deriving the Supply Curve
notes.content:
• Law of supply: other things remaining constant, as the price of a commodity rises, its quantity supplied rises, and as price falls, quantity supplied falls — a direct (positive) relationship between price and quantity supplied.
• Assumptions: cost of production constant; technology constant; no change in government policy; prices of related goods constant; no change in number of sellers; no expectations of price change; no change in natural conditions.
• Why does the supply curve slope upward?
– Higher price means higher profit, encouraging firms to produce more.
– Law of increasing marginal cost (diminishing returns) — more output is produced only at higher prices.
– New firms enter the industry at higher prices.
– Higher price enables use of costlier inputs.
– Producers can shift resources from other products.
• Exceptions to the law of supply (backward-bending or vertical/downward supply curves):
– Agricultural goods — supply depends on the season/rainfall, not price in the short run.
– Perishable goods — must be sold soon whatever the price.
– Rare and artistic goods (antiques, paintings) — supply cannot be increased.
– Labour supply — at very high wage rates workers may prefer leisure, so the labour supply curve bends backward.
– Expectation of price rise — sellers withhold supply; expectation of fall — sell more now.
– Goods with fixed supply, and sellers in need of immediate cash, also behave contrary to the law.
• Supply curve: upward sloping from left to right. Individual supply curve — one firm; market supply curve is the horizontal sum of all individual supply curves.
• Derivation of supply curve: from the supply schedule by plotting price (Y) vs quantity supplied (X). In perfect competition, the firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of its MC curve above the AVC minimum (shutdown point).

notes.title: 4.3 Change in Quantity Supplied (Movement along SC) vs Change in Supply (Shift in SC)
notes.content:
• Change in quantity supplied: caused only by a change in the price of the good; shown by movement along the same supply curve. Expansion of supply (price rises, supply rises — upward movement); contraction of supply (price falls — downward movement).
• Change in supply: caused by changes in non-price factors; shown by shift of the whole supply curve. Increase in supply — rightward shift (technology improves, input prices fall, subsidy, more firms). Decrease in supply — leftward shift (higher input costs, taxes, bad weather, fewer firms).
[TABLE]
Basis | Change in Quantity Supplied | Change in Supply
Cause | Own price | Other factors
Curve | Movement along same SC | Shift of SC
Terms | Expansion / Contraction | Increase / Decrease
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 4.4 Market Equilibrium — Invisible Hand; Effects of Shifts in DC and SC
notes.content:
• Market equilibrium: the situation where quantity demanded = quantity supplied at a particular price. That price is the equilibrium (market-clearing) price and the quantity is the equilibrium quantity. Represented by the point of intersection of the demand and supply curves.
• Example:
[TABLE]
Price (Rs.) | Demand | Supply | Position
10 | 20 | 80 | Surplus 60 (excess supply)
8 | 40 | 60 | Surplus 20
6 | 50 | 50 | Equilibrium
4 | 70 | 30 | Shortage 40 (excess demand)
[/TABLE]
• Surplus (excess supply): at a price above equilibrium, Qs > Qd — competition among sellers pushes price down.
• Shortage (excess demand): at a price below equilibrium, Qd > Qs — competition among buyers pushes price up.
• Stable equilibrium: forces automatically restore the equilibrium after a disturbance. Unstable equilibrium: forces push away from equilibrium.
• The Invisible Hand (Adam Smith): individuals, pursuing their own self-interest, are led as if by an "invisible hand" to promote the interest of society through the price mechanism — without central direction, markets allocate resources to their most valued uses. Prices act as signals.
• Effects of shifts on equilibrium:
[TABLE]
Change | Effect on Price | Effect on Quantity
Demand increases (SC constant) | Rises | Rises
Demand decreases (SC constant) | Falls | Falls
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Change | Effect on Price | Effect on Quantity
Supply increases (DC constant) | Falls | Rises
Supply decreases (DC constant) | Rises | Falls
Both D and S increase | Uncertain | Rises
Both D and S decrease | Uncertain | Falls
D increases, S decreases | Rises | Uncertain
D decreases, S increases | Falls | Uncertain
[/TABLE]
• Simultaneous shifts: if demand and supply increase by the same proportion, price remains unchanged and quantity rises.
• Price controls: Price ceiling (maximum price below equilibrium, e.g. rent control, essential commodities) creates shortage and black markets. Price floor (minimum price above equilibrium, e.g. Minimum Support Price, minimum wage) creates surplus.
• Algebraic solution: if Qd = 100 − 5P and Qs = 20 + 3P, equilibrium: 100 − 5P = 20 + 3P, so 8P = 80, P = 10, Q = 50.

notes.title: 4.5 Elasticity of Supply and its Application
notes.content:
• Elasticity of supply (Es): degree of responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price. Es = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q). It is positive due to direct relation.
• Types:
[TABLE]
Type | Value | Curve | Meaning
Perfectly elastic | Es = ∞ | Horizontal line | Supply infinite at a given price
Perfectly inelastic | Es = 0 | Vertical line | Supply fixed regardless of price
Unitary elastic | Es = 1 | Straight line from origin | % change Q = % change P
Relatively elastic | Es > 1 | Straight line cutting the price (Y) axis | Q changes proportionately more
Relatively inelastic | Es < 1 | Cuts the quantity (X) axis | Q changes proportionately less
[/TABLE]
• Geometric rule for a straight-line supply curve: if it passes through the origin Es = 1; if it cuts the Y-axis, Es > 1; if it cuts the X-axis, Es < 1 (regardless of slope).
• Factors affecting elasticity of supply: nature of the good (perishable — inelastic; durable — elastic); time period (market period — perfectly inelastic; short run — inelastic; long run — elastic); cost of production (rising cost — inelastic supply); availability of inputs/spare capacity; technology; mobility of factors; stocks (storable goods are elastic); risk-taking ability; number of firms; government policy.
• Measurement methods: percentage method, point method, arc method.
• Numerical examples:
– Price rises from Rs. 10 to Rs. 12; supply rises from 100 to 130: %ΔQ = 30%, %ΔP = 20%, Es = 1.5 (elastic).
– Price rises from Rs. 20 to Rs. 22; supply rises from 50 to 52: %ΔQ = 4%, %ΔP = 10%, Es = 0.4 (inelastic).
• Applications: decides tax incidence (more of tax is borne by sellers with inelastic supply); helps in agricultural pricing and MSP; guides government on price stabilisation; helps firms in capacity planning; explains price volatility in agricultural markets (inelastic supply causes big price swings); important in international trade, factor pricing (supply of land is perfectly inelastic — economic rent), and wartime rationing.

notes.title: 5.1 Meaning and Definition of Production; Factors of Production
notes.content:
• Production: the process of creating or adding utility (value) to goods and services — transforming inputs into outputs. Production does not mean creation of matter; it means creation of utility (form, place, time, service utility).
• Output = quantity produced; input = resources used.
• Factors of Production:
– 1. Land: all natural resources — soil, minerals, forests, water, climate. Features: gift of nature; fixed in supply (perfectly inelastic in total); passive factor; heterogeneous in fertility and location; immobile geographically. Reward: rent.
– 2. Labour: physical and mental human effort for a reward. Features: perishable; inseparable from labourer; active; varies in efficiency; weak bargaining power; supply is affected by population and wage rate. Reward: wages.
– 3. Capital: man-made goods used for further production (machines, tools, buildings, money capital, working capital). Features: produced factor; passive; mobile; depreciates. Reward: interest. Capital formation requires saving, mobilisation and investment.
– 4. Entrepreneur / Organisation: coordinates other factors, takes decisions and bears risk and uncertainty. Functions: initiative, risk-bearing, innovation (Schumpeter), management, decision making. Reward: profit.
• Types of capital: fixed vs circulating; physical vs human; private vs social.
• Division of labour: splitting of production into small tasks — raises efficiency; limits: size of the market.

notes.title: 5.2 Production Function — One Variable and Two Variable Inputs
notes.content:
• Production function: the technical relationship between physical inputs and the maximum output that can be produced with a given state of technology. Q = f(L, K, N, O …), where Q = output; L = labour; K = capital; N = land; O = organisation.
• Features: relates to a given period; assumes a given technology (change in technology shifts the function); shows the maximum output from given inputs (efficiency); inputs must be used in efficient combinations; defined for a specific product.
• Short run: a period in which at least one factor is fixed (usually capital); output can be changed only by changing variable factors (labour, raw material). Long run: a period in which all factors are variable. Very long run: technology also changes.
• Production function with one variable input (short run): Q = f(L), with K fixed. Studied through Total Product (TP), Average Product (AP) and Marginal Product (MP).
– TP: total output from all units of the variable input.
– AP = TP ÷ L.
– MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL or TPn − TPn−1.
• Production function with two variable inputs (long run): Q = f(L, K), studied through isoquants and returns to scale.
• Cobb–Douglas production function: Q = A·Lα·Kβ — α and β are output elasticities of labour and capital. If α + β = 1, constant returns to scale; >1 increasing; <1 decreasing. Suited to two-factor analysis.
• Fixed proportion (Leontief) production function: inputs used in fixed ratios (L-shaped isoquants).

notes.title: 5.3 Short-Run Production Function — Law of Variable Proportion
notes.content:
• Law of Variable Proportions (Law of Diminishing Returns): when more and more units of a variable factor are applied to a given quantity of fixed factors, the total product initially increases at an increasing rate, then at a diminishing rate, reaches a maximum, and finally declines; MP first rises, then falls and eventually becomes negative.
• Assumptions: technology constant; at least one factor is fixed; variable factors are homogeneous; the possibility of varying factor proportions exists; short-run phenomenon.
• Illustration (fixed land = 1 hectare):
[TABLE]
Labour | TP | AP | MP | Stage
1 | 10 | 10 | 10 | I
2 | 24 | 12 | 14 | I
3 | 39 | 13 | 15 | I (MP max)
4 | 52 | 13 | 13 | II (AP max, AP = MP)
5 | 60 | 12 | 8 | II
6 | 64 | 10.7 | 4 | II
7 | 64 | 9.1 | 0 | End of II (TP max)
8 | 60 | 7.5 | −4 | III
[/TABLE]
• Relationship between TP, AP and MP:
– MP rises, reaches a maximum and then falls; TP increases at an increasing rate while MP rises, and at a diminishing rate once MP falls.
– When MP = 0, TP is maximum. When MP < 0, TP falls.
– MP cuts AP at AP's maximum point. When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP < AP, AP falls.
– AP and MP both start equal for the first unit.
• Three stages of production:
– Stage I — Increasing returns: from origin to the point where AP is maximum (MP = AP). Not a rational stage to stop — fixed factors underutilised.
– Stage II — Diminishing returns: from maximum AP to the point where MP = 0 (TP maximum). The rational stage of production — the firm operates here.
– Stage III — Negative returns: MP < 0, TP falls. A rational producer never operates here.
• Causes of increasing returns: better utilisation of fixed factors; division of labour and specialisation. Causes of diminishing returns: overuse of fixed factor; imperfect substitutability of factors; poor coordination. Causes of negative returns: overcrowding and managerial inefficiency.
• Applicability: originally for agriculture (Ricardo, Malthus); applies to all production activities. Delayed by better technology, but not avoided.

notes.title: 5.4 Long-Run Production Function — Law of Returns to Scale
notes.content:
• Returns to scale: how output changes when all inputs are changed in the same proportion (the scale changes), in the long run.
• Three types:
– Increasing returns to scale (IRS): output rises by a larger proportion than inputs (inputs double, output more than doubles). Causes: division of labour, indivisibility of factors, technical economies, managerial economies, marketing economies.
– Constant returns to scale (CRS): output rises in the same proportion (inputs double, output doubles). Typical when internal economies and diseconomies offset each other. Cobb–Douglas with α + β = 1.
– Decreasing returns to scale (DRS): output rises by a smaller proportion (inputs double, output less than doubles). Causes: managerial diseconomies, coordination problems, labour disputes, exhaustion of natural resources.
[TABLE]
Scale | Labour + Capital | Output | % change in output vs inputs
1 | 1 + 1 | 100 | —
2 | 2 + 2 | 250 | 150% vs 100% — IRS
3 | 3 + 3 | 400 | 60% vs 50% — IRS
4 | 4 + 4 | 520 | 30% vs 33% — DRS
[/TABLE]
• Difference between returns to scale and returns to a factor (variable proportions): returns to scale — all inputs change, long run, scale changes, factor proportions unchanged; variable proportions — one factor changes, short run, proportions change.
• Typical firm: IRS first, then CRS over a range, then DRS.

notes.title: 5.5 Isoquant Curve
notes.content:
• Isoquant (iso-product curve/equal-product curve): a curve showing all possible combinations of two inputs (labour and capital) that yield the same level of output.
• Isoquant map: set of isoquants; a higher isoquant means higher output.
• Example (output = 100 units):
[TABLE]
Combination | Labour | Capital
A | 1 | 12
B | 2 | 8
C | 3 | 5
D | 4 | 3
E | 5 | 2
[/TABLE]
• Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTSLK): the rate at which one input can be substituted for another without changing output; MRTS = −ΔK/ΔL = MPL/MPK. Diminishes along an isoquant.
• Properties: slopes downward; convex to the origin (diminishing MRTS); two isoquants never intersect; higher isoquant means more output; do not touch the axes; not necessarily parallel.
• Types/shapes: Linear (perfect substitutes); L-shaped (perfect complements/fixed proportions — Leontief); Convex (imperfect substitutes — typical); Kinked (activity analysis — a few techniques).
• Ridge lines: lines that mark the boundary of the economic region (where MP of an input is zero). The economic region of production is the area between ridge lines, where isoquants are downward sloping.
• Isoquant vs indifference curve: isoquants measure physical output (cardinal, can be labelled 100, 200); ICs measure satisfaction (ordinal). Both are convex and non-intersecting.
• Marginal rate of substitution vs MRTS: MRS relates to consumers (utility); MRTS relates to producers (output).

notes.title: 6.1 Meaning, Concepts, Short-Run and Long-Run Cost Functions
notes.content:
• Cost: the expenditure incurred in producing a good or service. Cost function: C = f(Q, T, Pf) — relation between cost and output, technology and input prices.
• Cost concepts:
– Money (nominal) cost: total expenditure in money terms. Real cost: effort and sacrifice of the factor owners (Marshall: pains of labour, abstinence of capital).
– Opportunity cost: value of the next best alternative forgone.
– Explicit costs: actual out-of-pocket payments (wages, rent, raw materials). Implicit costs: imputed cost of self-owned resources (owner's own labour, own capital, own building) — not paid in cash.
– Accounting cost = explicit cost only. Economic cost = explicit + implicit (including normal profit).
– Fixed costs (FC/TFC): do not change with output in the short run (rent, insurance, salaries, depreciation) — also called overhead/supplementary cost. Variable costs (VC): change with output (raw materials, wages of casual labour, power) — prime cost.
– Sunk cost: already spent and unrecoverable; irrelevant to future decisions. Incremental cost: change in total cost from a decision. Marginal cost: addition to total cost for one more unit.
– Private cost vs Social cost: social cost includes externalities (e.g. pollution). Historical vs replacement cost. Out-of-pocket vs book cost. Controllable vs uncontrollable cost. Direct vs indirect cost.
• Short-run cost functions (at least one factor fixed):
– TFC: constant at all outputs. TVC: rises with output. TC = TFC + TVC.
– AFC = TFC/Q — falls continuously, rectangular hyperbola shape. AVC = TVC/Q — U-shaped. ATC (AC) = TC/Q = AFC + AVC — U-shaped. MC = ΔTC/ΔQ = ΔTVC/ΔQ — U-shaped (not influenced by TFC).
• Illustration:
[TABLE]
Q | TFC | TVC | TC | AFC | AVC | AC | MC
0 | 60 | 0 | 60 | — | — | — | —
1 | 60 | 30 | 90 | 60 | 30 | 90 | 30
2 | 60 | 50 | 110 | 30 | 25 | 55 | 20
3 | 60 | 66 | 126 | 20 | 22 | 42 | 16
4 | 60 | 88 | 148 | 15 | 22 | 37 | 22
5 | 60 | 120 | 180 | 12 | 24 | 36 | 32
6 | 60 | 168 | 228 | 10 | 28 | 38 | 48
[/TABLE]
• Relationships: MC curve cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points. When MC < AC, AC falls; when MC > AC, AC rises. AC = AFC + AVC, and the gap between AC and AVC shrinks with output but never vanishes. The AC minimum occurs at a higher output than the AVC minimum. U-shape is due to the law of variable proportions (increasing returns, then diminishing returns).
• Long-run cost functions: all costs are variable; no fixed cost.
– Long-run Average Cost (LAC): envelope curve to all short-run average cost (SAC) curves — tangent to each SAC curve (but not at the minimum points of the SAC except at the minimum point of LAC). U-shaped but flatter than SAC, because of economies and diseconomies of scale (not the law of variable proportions). Also called the planning curve.
– Long-run Marginal Cost (LMC): derived from short-run marginal costs; cuts LAC at its minimum; flatter than SMC.
– Minimum efficient scale (MES): lowest output at which LAC is minimised.

notes.title: 6.2 Economies of Scale and Scope
notes.content:
• Economies of scale: reduction in average cost as output expands (scale of production rises).
• Internal economies (arise within the firm due to its own expansion):
– Technical: large machines, specialisation, indivisibility. Managerial: specialised managers. Marketing: bulk advertising and distribution. Financial: cheaper credit. Risk-bearing: diversification. Labour: division of labour. Purchasing: bulk discounts.
• External economies (arise outside the firm, from growth of the industry): infrastructure, skilled labour pool, ancillary industries, shared research, information, transport — typically in industrial clusters (e.g. Tirupur, Surat).
• Diseconomies of scale: rise in AC when the firm becomes too large — management coordination problems, labour disputes, red tape, scarce inputs. External diseconomies: congestion, pollution, rising input prices.
• Economies of scope: reduction in average cost when a firm produces a variety of related products together rather than separately (shared inputs: equipment, brand, distribution, R&D) — e.g. a dairy producing milk, curd and butter; a bank offering several services.
– Difference: scale — about the volume of one product; scope — about the variety of products.

notes.title: 6.3 Concepts of Revenue and Profit Determination
notes.content:
• Total Revenue (TR) = P × Q. Average Revenue (AR) = TR/Q = P (AR is the demand curve). Marginal Revenue (MR) = ΔTR/ΔQ.
• Under perfect competition: price is constant; AR = MR = P (horizontal line); TR is a straight line from the origin.
• Under imperfect competition (monopoly, etc.): AR slopes downward; MR lies below AR (for a straight-line AR, MR has twice the slope and cuts the quantity axis at half the distance). TR rises, reaches a maximum when MR = 0 (Ed = 1), then falls.
• MR–AR–elasticity relation: MR = AR × (e − 1)/e, and e = AR/(AR − MR).
• Profit: π = TR − TC.
– Normal profit: minimum return required to keep the entrepreneur in business; part of economic cost (AR = AC).
– Supernormal (abnormal/economic) profit: TR − TC > 0 beyond normal profit (AR > AC).
– Loss: TR < TC (AR < AC).
– Break-even point: TR = TC (AR = AC; zero economic profit).
– Shutdown point: price falls below minimum AVC — the firm should stop production in the short run (loses only fixed cost). If AR ≥ AVC but < AC, the firm continues to produce in the short run, minimising loss.
• Profit determination (two approaches):
– TR–TC approach: profit is maximum where the vertical gap between TR and TC is greatest.
– MR–MC approach: profit is maximum at output where MR = MC and MC cuts MR from below (MC slope greater than MR slope).
• Profit maximisation vs other goals: sales maximisation (Baumol), managerial utility (Williamson), satisficing (Simon), growth.

notes.title: 6.4 Isocost Line
notes.content:
• Isocost line (equal-cost line): shows all combinations of two inputs (labour and capital) that a firm can buy with a given total cost (outlay) and given factor prices. TC = w·L + r·K (w = wage rate, r = rental rate of capital).
• Intercepts: TC/w on the labour axis; TC/r on the capital axis. Slope = −w/r (ratio of factor prices).
• Shifts: increase in outlay — parallel outward shift; decrease — inward; change in w — rotates around the capital-axis intercept; change in r — rotates around the labour-axis intercept.
• Analogy: isocost is to the producer what the budget line is to the consumer.

notes.title: 6.5 Producer's Equilibrium
notes.content:
• Producer's equilibrium: the combination of factors that gives the producer maximum output at given cost or minimum cost for a given output (least-cost combination).
• Conditions (shown by tangency of isoquant and isocost line):
– First-order condition: MRTSLK = w/r (slope of isoquant = slope of isocost), which is MPL/MPK = w/r, or MPL/w = MPK/r.
– Second-order condition: isoquant must be convex to the origin at the equilibrium point.
• Two approaches:
– Maximising output subject to a cost constraint: reach the highest isoquant within the given isocost line.
– Minimising cost for a given output: reach the lowest isocost line touching the given isoquant.
• Expansion path: locus of producer's equilibrium points as outlay (cost) rises with constant factor prices — shows the least-cost combination for different output levels.
• Effect of change in factor prices: if wages rise relative to the price of capital, the firm substitutes capital for labour (new tangency on a steeper isocost line).
• Difference between consumer's and producer's equilibrium: consumer maximises satisfaction (ordinal); producer maximises output (cardinal).

notes.title: 7.1 Meaning and Definition of Market; Types of Market
notes.content:
• Market: in economics, any arrangement (place, physical or virtual) in which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services at a price. It need not be a specific place. Cournot: "Market means not any particular market place in which things are bought and sold but the whole of any region in which buyers and sellers are in such free intercourse with one another that the prices of the same goods tend to equality easily and quickly."
• Essentials of a market: a commodity; buyers and sellers; contact between them; a price; competition.
• Classification of markets:
– By area: local, regional, national, international.
– By time (Marshall): very short period (market period), short period, long period, very long period (secular).
– By nature of transactions: spot and future markets.
– By volume of business: wholesale and retail.
– By competition (most important): perfect competition and imperfect competition (monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, duopoly; also monopsony, oligopsony).
• Market structure depends on: number of buyers and sellers, nature of the product (homogeneous/differentiated), freedom of entry and exit, knowledge of market, mobility of factors, and control over price.
[TABLE]
Feature | Perfect Competition | Monopolistic Competition | Oligopoly | Monopoly
Number of sellers | Very large | Many | Few | One
Product | Homogeneous | Differentiated | Homogeneous or differentiated | Unique, no close substitute
Entry/exit | Free | Free | Restricted | Blocked
Price control | None (price taker) | Some | Considerable (interdependent) | Considerable (price maker, but limited by demand)
Demand curve | Horizontal | Downward, elastic | Kinked/indeterminate | Downward, less elastic
Selling cost | None | Heavy | Heavy | Little/Some
Example | Wheat in a mandi | Soaps, restaurants | Cars, telecom, airlines | Indian Railways
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 7.2 Perfect and Imperfect Competition; Features of Perfect Competition
notes.content:
• Perfect competition — features:
– Large number of buyers and sellers — no one can influence price.
– Homogeneous (identical) product.
– Free entry and exit of firms.
– Perfect knowledge of the market conditions among buyers and sellers.
– Perfect mobility of factors of production.
– No government intervention; no transport costs.
– Firm is a price taker, industry is the price maker; uniform price prevails; AR = MR = Price (horizontal demand curve for the firm).
– Absence of selling cost.
• Pure competition is a narrower concept (features 1–3 only); perfect competition includes all features.
• Price determination in perfect competition: by interaction of industry demand and industry supply. The firm accepts that price.
• Short-run equilibrium of the firm: condition MR = MC, with MC cutting MR from below. Three outcomes: supernormal profit (P > AC), normal profit (P = AC) and loss (P < AC but ≥ AVC). Shutdown if P < AVC. Firm's short-run supply curve = MC above minimum AVC.
• Long-run equilibrium: free entry and exit make firms earn only normal profit: P = MR = SMC = SAC = LMC = LAC (minimum LAC). Firm produces at the optimum scale — maximum productive and allocative efficiency (P = MC). If supernormal profits exist, new firms enter and price falls; if losses, firms exit and price rises. Industry supply curve: constant-, increasing- or decreasing-cost industry.
• Merits: efficient allocation; consumer sovereignty; no exploitation; lowest price; optimum output. Demerits: unrealistic; no innovation or product variety; no economies of scale benefit beyond a limit; no advertising information.
• Imperfect competition: any market where one or more of the conditions of perfect competition is not fulfilled — sellers have some control over price. Includes monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly.

notes.title: 7.3 Monopoly, Oligopoly and Monopolistic Competition — Basics and Features
notes.content:
• Monopoly (mono = single, poly = seller): a market with a single seller of a product having no close substitutes, with barriers to entry.
– Features: single seller (firm = industry); no close substitutes; strong barriers to entry; firm is a price maker; downward-sloping AR curve with MR below AR; price discrimination possible; supernormal profits can persist in the long run; control over supply.
– Sources/causes of monopoly: exclusive ownership of raw materials; patents and copyrights; government licence/franchise (public utilities); economies of scale (natural monopoly — electricity distribution, railways); mergers and cartels; control over technology; brand loyalty.
– Equilibrium: MR = MC with MC cutting MR from below; price is read from the AR curve above MC (so P > MC). Profit = (AR − AC) × Q. A monopolist produces where demand is elastic (MR > 0).
– Price discrimination: selling the same product at different prices to different buyers not justified by cost differences. Conditions: monopoly power; markets can be separated; elasticities differ; no resale. Degrees: first (perfect — each buyer charged the maximum price), second (block pricing), third (different groups/markets). Equilibrium: MR in each market is equal to common MC (MR1 = MR2 = MC); charge higher price in the market with less elastic demand.
– Merits: economies of scale; funds for R&D and innovation; natural monopolies can be efficient; Demerits: higher price and lower output than competition; exploitation; deadweight loss; X-inefficiency; inequality.
– Regulation: price control, anti-trust law (Competition Act 2002 in India — CCI), nationalisation, taxation.
• Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin, Joan Robinson, 1933): many sellers selling differentiated but closely related (substitute) products.
– Features: large number of sellers (smaller than in perfect competition); product differentiation (brand, quality, design, packaging); free entry and exit; selling costs (advertising) significant; some control over price; downward-sloping, highly elastic demand; non-price competition; imperfect knowledge.
– Short-run equilibrium: MR = MC; firm may earn supernormal profit, normal profit or loss. Long-run equilibrium: entry/exit eliminates supernormal profit; AR is tangent to LAC at a point on the falling portion of LAC: P = AC > MC. Result: excess capacity (production below the optimum output) — the cost of variety. Group instead of industry. Tangency solution (Chamberlin).
• Oligopoly (oligos = few): market with a few large sellers, each aware of rivals' reactions.
– Types: pure/perfect oligopoly (homogeneous — cement, steel) vs differentiated/imperfect oligopoly (cars, mobile phones); collusive vs non-collusive; open vs closed; duopoly (two sellers).
– Features: few sellers; interdependence (each firm's decision depends on rivals' reactions); barriers to entry; price rigidity (stickiness); heavy advertising and selling costs; non-price competition; indeterminate demand curve; group behaviour; presence of price leadership; uncertainty.
– Kinked demand curve (Sweezy, 1939): explains price rigidity. If a firm raises price, rivals do not follow — demand is elastic; if it cuts price, rivals follow — demand is inelastic. The demand curve has a kink at the prevailing price and MR has a vertical (discontinuous) gap; MC can vary within the gap without changing price/output.
– Collusive oligopoly: cartel (formal agreement — OPEC), price leadership (dominant firm/barometric), price-fixing, market sharing; illegal in many countries.
– Game theory (Neumann–Morgenstern): Prisoner's dilemma — each firm's dominant strategy (cut price/advertise) leads to a worse joint outcome (Nash equilibrium).
– Cournot duopoly model (1838): two firms, each assumes the rival's output is fixed. Bertrand model: firms compete on price.
• Other forms: monopsony (single buyer), oligopsony (few buyers), bilateral monopoly (single seller meets single buyer).
• Comparison — Perfect competition vs monopoly: perfect competition: P = MC, output higher, price lower, normal profit, efficient; monopoly: P > MC, output lower, price higher, supernormal profit, deadweight loss.
